newsitem.title: USA: Healthdyne Technologies set for proxy fight.
newsitem.headline: Healthdyne Technologies set for proxy fight.

text.p: Medical device firm Invacare Corp. will tackle the next step in its six-month-old hostile bid for Healthdyne Technologies Inc. on Wednesday when it tries to take over Healthdyne's board of directors at the company's annual shareholders meeting.
Wall Street experts predict a close vote at the session, which will be critical for the future of both firms. The meeting will be held in Healthdyne's home town of Marietta, Ga.

Although Invacare's $200 million offer is small compared with the billion dollar mergers that occur practically daily in corporate America, the Healthdyne-Invacare fight has raised significant takeover issues.

Healthdyne has repeatedly rejected Invacare's offer, valued at $15 per share, and last week annnounced that an unidentified company may be willing to pay more. Invacare originally offered $12.50 per share in January and then raised the bid three times.
Meanwhile, shares of Healthdyne have soared to about $17 per share from a January price of about $9 on views that the company will be sold for more than Invacare's $15 offer.
Healthdyne specializes in devices for respiratory and sleep disorders.

At the meeting, shareholders will be asked to re-elect Healthdyne's seven-member board or vote in a dissident four-member slate offered by Invacare. A 50 percent majority of voting shares is needed for victory.
Both companies have been pressing their case with shareholders over the past few weeks.

Invacare has said its slate would immediately conduct an auction of the company and would consider bids other than the $15 offer now on the table. The company also has stressed that its nominees would be independent directors with no ties to Invacare.
At the meeting, shareholders are not being asked to consider Invacare's $15 per share offer. The tender offer is set to expire on Aug. 1.

Independent proxy firm Instiutional Shareholder Services has recommended shareholders re-elect the Healthdyne board, saying that a board controlled by a dissident group would cause upheaval at Healthdyne. But the Maryland-based group also expressed concern about Healthdyne's committment to completing a transaction with another party, noting there is no assurance that a deal will take place.

Wall Street experts estimate that Invacare may already hold some 40 percent of the shareholder vote, including the 600,000 shares it owned as of the June 23 record date and those held by traders who play takeover stocks.

Although Invacare has insisted it will not raise its bid again, the company could be forced to reconsider its position if its nominees are elected to the board and a higher offer is submitted by another party.
"I would say that $15 is not the final offer," said Matthew Dodds, analyst at Dillon Read & Co. Inc.

In the months since Invacare launched the takeover, Healthdyne has posted improved earnings, which has prompted some Wall Street analysts to speculate it may be worth $20 per share. Meanwhile, Invacare last week admitted said its sales growth has been hurt by lower sales and pricing pressures.
Over the past six months, the fight for control of Healthdyne has been accompanied by some twists and turns that have drawn attention from merger experts

Early in the takeover battle, the Georgia legislature considered a measure that would have required all companies incorporated in the state to have staggered board terms -- a move that would have protected Healthdyne from Invacare's efforts to take control of the board. The legislature eventually dropped the issue.

Earlier this month, a U.S. District Court judge upheld a portion of Healthdyne's shareholder rights plan that prohibits new directors from overturning the plan, known as a "poison pill". Known as a "continuing directors" or "deadhand" provision, the measure is a defense against hostile takeovers.
